Combining LLM orchestration, SMT solving, and Lean 4 theorem proving to build a self-correcting verification pipeline.
The Bottleneck of AI Coding Agents
Autonomous AI coding agents have changed how we start software projects. Devin, Cursor, Claude Code, and their open-source siblings can scaffold an entire feature from a one-line prompt. For many tasks, this is a genuine productivity boost.
But anyone who has shipped production code knows the gap: syntactically valid code is not the same as correct code. A generated function can look idiomatic, pass a few unit tests, and still violate the implicit safety property that actually matters – a state transition happening before authorization, an arithmetic overflow on a specific bit width, a reentrancy hole in a smart contract, or a missing compliance check in a financial workflow.
Tests only sample. They cannot exhaust the space of all inputs, all interleavings, and all edge cases. If we want AI agents that write the code we trust for infrastructure, finance, or safety-critical systems, we need something stronger than prompt engineering and test coverage.
We need the agent to prove what it wrote.
(That said, the accuracy of AI coding agents is steadily improving; it is unlikely that raw, unguarded models will be used as-is, and the kind of verification framework described here may well be folded into them over time.)
The 「Looks Correct But Is Broken」 Problem
In our paper, we describe the central failure pattern of LLM-generated code as 「looks correct but is broken.」 A model produces code that manipulates the right vocabulary, uses plausible variable names, and even passes surface-level tests, yet it skips a protocol step or misorders an effect.
A concrete example from our case studies is an ownership-transfer workflow. A naive generated hostile_takeover path tries to move an asset directly to Transferred from Idle, bypassing the required propose → accept state machine. It looks right at a glance, but Mumei rejects it with a temporal-effect violation:
InvalidPreState: ‘accept’ requires 'PendingTransfer'
but current state is 'Idle'
Counter-example: hostile_takeover(attacker=42)
The model did not 「know」 the protocol. It only knew the vocabulary. Without an explicit contract and a verifier, that mistake reaches production.
The Mumei Forge: A Stack, Not a Single Tool
Mumei treats every function-like unit as a proof obligation called an atom. An atom carries preconditions (requires:), postconditions (ensures:), a body, and a proof result. The goal is not to replace theorem provers with LLMs, but to put the LLM inside a loop where it is not the authority. The LLM proposes; the compiler and proof backends decide.
We use a forging metaphor on purpose. An atom is a blade, the compiler is the anvil, Z3 and Lean are the proving fire, and the agent is the blacksmith. The blacksmith does not write code and hope. It repeatedly heats, strikes, inspects, and repairs until the artifact satisfies its contract.
The pipeline looks like this:
Press enter or click to view image in full size

Figure 1: The Mumei verification pipeline – from user intent through the agent, compiler, Z3, and optional Lean escalation.
1. User intent / spec → mumei-agent
2. mumei-agent forges a candidate .mm atom or module
3. mumei parses, resolves, monomorphizes, lowers to HIR/MIR,
and runs verification
4. Z3 discharges the obligation:
・unsat → verified; emit LLVM IR, C headers, or verified JSON
・sat → concrete counter-example; return to agent for repair
・unknown → produce a proof certificate and escalate to Lean
5. Lean 4 (mumei-lean) proves the harder obligation and returns a .lean-cert.json
6. The certificate is consumed by the compiler or stored for future reuseThe layers are deliberately separable. The core compiler can verify code without the agent. The agent can call the compiler as a subprocess or through MCP. Lean escalation is optional and consumes certificates rather than requiring changes to the compiler core.
Step 1: Spec-Driven, Contract-Defined Code Generation
The loop starts with a high-level spec – a user requirement written in natural language or structured intent. mumei-agent does not emit raw Python or C++; it emits Mumei code, a small language where the boundaries of correctness are explicit from the start.
A spec captures intent. A contract makes that intent machine-checkable. Every atom carries requires: preconditions, ensures: postconditions, and a body: implementation. The compiler extracts verification conditions directly from the contract, so the gap between 「what we meant」 and 「what the code does」 is closed at generation time.
Here is a simple balance-transfer atom:
atom execute_settlement(
sender_balance: i64,
receiver_balance: i64,
amount: i64
) -> i64
requires: sender_balance >= 0
&& receiver_balance >= 0
&& amount > 0
&& sender_balance >= amount;
ensures: result == sender_balance + receiver_balance;
body: {
let new_sender = sender_balance - amount;
let new_receiver = receiver_balance + amount;
new_sender + new_receiver
};The requires: clause bounds the legal input space. The ensures: clause states the property that must hold afterward. The body: is the implementation. Because the contract is part of the language, the compiler can extract verification conditions automatically instead of asking a human to annotate a foreign language.
Step 2: MIR Analysis and Counter-Example Guided Repair
The mumei compiler lowers the atom into Mid-level IR and performs analyses including liveness, move analysis, and linearity checks. It then generates verification conditions for Z3.
The verification pass is conceptually simple:
pub fn verify_atom(mir: &MIRAtom) -> VerificationResult {
let mut solver = Z3Solver::new();
solver.assert(&mir.preconditions);
solver.assert(&mir.body_logic);
solver.assert_not(&mir.postconditions); // search for a violation match solver.check() {
SMTResult::Unsat => VerificationResult::Verified,
SMTResult::Sat(ce) => VerificationResult::CounterExample(ce),
SMTResult::Unknown => VerificationResult::NeedsLean,
}
}
If Z3 returns sat, it produces a concrete counter-example – the exact input values that break the contract. Instead of asking the LLM to “try again,” mumei-agent receives the precise failing state and repairs the code deterministically. This is not heuristic re-prompting; it is counter-example guided self-healing.
Step 3: When SMT Is Not Enough, Escalate to Lean 4
SMT solvers are fast, but they can time out or return unknown on obligations involving induction, unbounded loops, or complex algebraic properties. For those cases, Mumei exports a proof certificate to mumei-lean, which translates the obligation into Lean 4 and attempts a formal proof.
For the settlement atom, the generated Lean obligation is straightforward:
theorem execute_settlement_preserves_total_balance
(sender receiver amount : Int)
(h_pre : sender >= 0 ∧ receiver >= 0 ∧ amount > 0 ∧ sender >= amount) :
(sender - amount) + (receiver + amount) = sender + receiver := by
omegaOnce Lean’s kernel accepts the proof term, the atom receives a lean_verified certificate and can be trusted as a reusable building block. Over time, the standard library becomes a cache of forged, proven components for future agents and applications.
Results and Current Status
The key difference between a plain LLM loop and the Mumei loop is not speed; it is the shape of the feedback.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

As of our latest benchmark snapshot (2026–06–02), the Mumei standard library contains 54 modules, 325 atoms, 320 Z3-proven atoms, 5 reviewed trusted atoms, and a weighted health score of 0.997. The trusted atoms are explicitly marked and reviewed; every other atom is backed by an SMT or Lean proof.
These numbers matter because they show the pipeline is not a research demo. It is a working, expanding library where correctness is the default.
What This Means for the Future
The future of AI-native software engineering is not just larger context windows or better prompts. It is compiler architectures designed for agents – systems where generation and verification are coupled, where a failed proof is treated as a training signal, and where correctness is an artifact, not an afterthought.
Mumei is a step in that direction. The current work already covers multi-file cross-spec verification, foreign-code audit flows, and the mumei-demo harness for reproducible safety audits. Near-term next steps include tighter MCP-based IDE integration and broader foreign-language coverage (Rust, Go, Python, Solidity).
If you are building infrastructure where a single missed edge case is unacceptable, probabilistic generation is no longer enough.
Current Scope and Limitations
Mumei is not yet a fully-fledged general-purpose programming language. Its guarantees hold only for properties explicitly stated in contracts, and current case studies – such as safe arithmetic, settlement, and ownership transfer – intentionally focus on a limited set of critical fragments. It is best understood as a “proof-of-constraint” toolchain for components that demand high leverage and high assurance; it is not intended as a replacement for existing languages, but rather as an attempt to explore that possibility at this stage.
Related Work: The Broader Shift Toward Verified AI Software
Mumei is not an isolated experiment. It sits at the intersection of several currents that are reshaping how we think about AI-generated software:

• Spec-Driven Development. Piskala (2026) argues that AI coding assistants make specifications, not code, the primary artifact, and proposes three levels of rigor: spec-first, spec-anchored, and spec-as-source. Mumei’s atoms – where requires/ensures clauses are compiled and verified – are a step toward spec-as-source: the contract is the source of truth and the body is a derived, checkable implementation.

• The Approximation Problem. Tratt (2022) observes that generative AI fills in incomplete specifications with learned approximations, but software cannot tolerate approximation. The missing piece is rigorous validation. Mumei’s loop supplies exactly that: every candidate is checked by Z3 or Lean before it can be accepted.

• AI + Formal Proof. DeepMind’s AlphaProof (2024) uses a pre-trained model to generate proof candidates in Lean, then lets the Lean kernel reject invalid ones. This is the same architecture Mumei-lean uses: candidate obligations generated by an agent are either discharged or counter-exampled by a trusted proof checker.

• The Mainstreaming of Formal Verification. Kleppmann (2025) predicts that LLMs will make formal verification economically viable for everyday software, creating 「vericoding」 as the antithesis of 「vibecoding.」 Mumei is a vericoding stack: the agent writes code, but the compiler and provers certify it.

• Theory Building as the Last Bottleneck. Hiroki (2026) argues that as coding becomes cheap, the remaining bottleneck moves upstream to problem definition and 「theory building」 – the deep, often tacit domain understanding that code and specs cannot fully capture. Mumei does not eliminate this work, but it encodes the resulting theory into machine-checkable contracts and proof certificates, turning fragile knowledge debt into reusable verification assets.
Taken together, these works suggest that AI-generated code needs a verification layer, and that verification layer must be as automated as the generation itself.
